children: shares sank nearly 7% at 10.20 a.m. ET on November 16 in regular trading, the first session since a court ruling on its memory business. U.S. District Judge Noel Wise in the Northern District of California denied a joint motion by Micron, Samsung and SK hynix to dismiss a proposed class action over conventional DRAM supply on November 14. The ruling does not decide whether the companies broke the law.

The complaint, filed June 25 by 17 consumers and small businesses, alleges the three suppliers cut conventional DRAM output from late 2022, shifted capacity to high-bandwidth memory, and adopted nearly identical customer-vetting practices in January 2026. Plaintiffs claim conventional DRAM prices rose 171.8% in the year through the third quarter of 2025. The judge found the vetting allegation strongly supported a plausible inference of an agreement, while rejecting other theories. Defendants must respond by December 7, and the first case management conference is set for January 12, 2027. Separately, Anthropic's filing shows Micron buying about $1 billion of shares in its IPO placement.

The legal risk is slow, but it targets the core of Micron's earnings power. GuruFocus shows a gross margin of about 81% and a forward P/E near 4, figures that signal how much the market already discounts today's pricing as peak-cycle. The GF Score of 96/100 reflects elite profitability, a near-debt-free balance sheet and strong growth, with momentum the weakest link. Shares trade about 14% below the $846.38 GF Value, a modestly undervalued reading. That discount looks less like a bargain and more like a price on cyclicality and now litigation. The December 7 response is the first procedural marker, but Micron's fiscal first-quarter report in December matters more for pricing trends.

title: Micron Stocks Sink Nearly 7% After Judge Lets DRAM Supply Lawsuit Proceed
